chunks: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from ʿAlī ibn Maʿbad, from Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam, who said:
I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام at Minā about five hundred expressions from theological discourse, and I began saying: “They say such and such.”
He said: “Then say: such and such.”

I said: “May I be sacrificed for you! This is the halal and this is the haram; I know that you are its master and that you are the most knowledgeable of the people concerning it, but this is theological discourse.”
So he said to me: “Woe to you, O Hishām! Allah, Blessed and Exalted, does not establish His proof over His creation by means of a proof who does not possess all that they need.”

key_terms.أَبَا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu ʿAbdillāh, a title of Imam al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام
key_terms.الْحَرَامُ: that which is forbidden in religion
key_terms.الْحَلَالُ: that which is permissible in religion
key_terms.بِحُجَّةٍ: through a Divine proof, an authoritative proof appointed over creation
key_terms.خَلْقِهِ: His creation, meaning all creatures under Divine responsibility
key_terms.صَاحِبُهُ: its true possessor or master, meaning the one with authoritative knowledge of it

ai.seo_question: Why must the Imam know all matters needed by the people, including theology?
ai.summary: This hadith affirms that the Divine proof over creation must possess complete knowledge of what people need, including matters of theological discourse as well as halal and haram. It highlights the comprehensive authority and knowledge of the Imam عليه السلام within Shia understanding of Imamate.
